pathophysiology.summary: Acute Coronary Syndrome (ACS) is acute myocardial ischaemia caused by reduced coronary blood flow, usually after atherosclerotic plaque erosion or rupture with thrombosis. Partial or transient occlusion causes Non-ST-Elevation Acute Coronary Syndrome (NSTE-ACS); persistent occlusion causes ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction (STEMI) or Acute Coronary Occlusion Myocardial Infarction (ACOMI).
keyMechanisms: Plaque disruption exposes thrombogenic material, activating platelets and coronary thrombosis.
ACOMI includes classic STEMI and non-ST-elevation occlusion equivalents such as posterior, right-ventricular and De Winter patterns, and selected Left Bundle Branch Block (LBBB) patterns.
High-Sensitivity Cardiac Troponin (hs-cTn) rises with myocardial necrosis and supports rapid rule-in or rule-out using assay-specific thresholds and serial deltas.
Acute ischaemia can cause Ventricular Fibrillation (VF), Ventricular Tachycardia (VT), acute heart failure, cardiogenic shock and mechanical complications.

symptoms: Severe retrosternal pain, pressure, tightness or burning lasting more than 20 minutes at rest, often radiating to the arm, neck, jaw, epigastrium or back.
Dyspnoea, diaphoresis, nausea, vomiting, presyncope or syncope; older adults, women and people with diabetes may present with isolated dyspnoea, fatigue, delirium or epigastric discomfort.
physicalSigns: Assess for cold clammy peripheries, hypotension, raised jugular venous pressure, bibasal crackles, a new systolic murmur and signs of shock or acute heart failure.
redFlags: ST-elevation or ACOMI-equivalent patterns on the initial Electrocardiogram (ECG).
Ongoing ischaemic pain, acute heart failure, cardiogenic shock or sustained arrhythmia requiring immediate invasive escalation.
Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest; do not use level of consciousness alone to determine emergency coronary angiography eligibility.
precipitants: Tobacco use, diabetes mellitus, hypertension, dyslipidaemia, premature family history, Spontaneous Coronary Artery Dissection (SCAD), coronary spasm or coronary embolism.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Abrupt maximal-onset tearing pain, back radiation, inter-arm Blood Pressure (BP) difference, pulse deficit or widened mediastinum; obtain urgent Computed Tomography (CT) aortography before antithrombotics.
Pleuritic pain, sudden dyspnoea, hypoxaemia, right-ventricular strain or deep-vein thrombosis features; arrange Computed Tomography Pulmonary Angiography (CTPA) or V/Q imaging.
Positional pleuritic pain, friction rub or diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression; use echocardiography and inflammatory markers.

differentials.condition: Type 2 myocardial infarction or non-ischaemic troponin rise
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Troponin elevation from supply-demand mismatch such as sepsis, tachyarrhythmia, severe anaemia or renal failure without acute plaque disruption.

ruleIn.expectedFinding: ST elevation, ACOMI equivalent, ST depression or T-wave inversion
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Obtain and interpret within 10 minutes of FMC; add right-sided and posterior leads when indicated.

clinicalManagement.title: First 10 minutes and initial resuscitation
actions: Obtain and interpret a 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes; place the patient on continuous cardiac monitoring with a defibrillator available.
Give Aspirin 300 mg orally, chewed or dissolved, unless contraindicated.
Give oxygen only when SpO2 is below 90%; titrate to avoid a saturation above 96%.
Use intravenous (IV) fentanyl or morphine increments for severe refractory pain when appropriate.
Exclude suspected aortic dissection before potent anticoagulant or secondary antiplatelet therapy.

clinicalManagement.title: STEMI/ACOMI reperfusion pathway
actions: Use primary PCI when FMC-to-device time is 120 minutes or less; use local door-in-door-out and transfer targets for non-PCI hospitals.
If PCI delay exceeds 120 minutes, give weight-adjusted fibrinolysis within 30 minutes of FMC with Unfractionated Heparin (UFH) or enoxaparin according to protocol.
Repeat ECG at 60–90 minutes after fibrinolysis; arrange rescue PCI for failed lysis and routine angiography after successful lysis.
Use Dual Antiplatelet Therapy (DAPT) and anticoagulation according to the selected reperfusion strategy; routine Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors are not recommended.

For cardiogenic shock, arrange immediate angiography with or without PCI; routine Intra-Aortic Balloon Pump (IABP) or Veno-Arterial Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation (VA-ECMO) is not recommended without refractory mechanical collapse.

clinicalManagement.title: NSTE-ACS pathway
actions: Start parenteral anticoagulation with UFH, enoxaparin, fondaparinux or the local ACS protocol.
Use an immediate invasive strategy within 2 hours for instability, refractory angina, shock, acute heart failure or severe arrhythmia.
Use an early invasive strategy within 24 hours for high-risk features; apply the retained guideline comparison where recommendations differ.
Use aspirin plus a P2Y12 inhibitor according to invasive strategy; give Prasugrel only after coronary anatomy is defined and PCI is intended.
Use ischaemia testing to guide angiography in lower-risk patients.

clinicalManagement.title: In-hospital and discharge optimisation
actions: Individualise DAPT duration and antithrombotic combinations, including oral anticoagulation and Proton Pump Inhibitor (PPI) protection when indicated.
Start high-intensity lipid lowering, assess beta-blocker and ACE inhibitor/ARB indications, and refer to cardiac rehabilitation.
Document low-risk discharge or completed revascularisation, stable haemodynamics, medication education, emergency return advice and cardiology follow-up.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Reperfusion indicated within 12 hours of symptom onset; prefer Primary Percutaneous Coronary Intervention (PCI) if First Medical Contact (FMC)-to-device time is 120 minutes or less, otherwise fibrinolysis within 30 minutes of FMC.
Immediate invasive strategy within 2 hours for refractory pain, instability, acute heart failure or cardiogenic shock.
Give supplemental oxygen only when oxygen saturation (SpO2) is below 90%; target 90–96%.

values: Very high risk within 2 h; high risk within 24 h

teaching.scope: Adult ACS assessment, reperfusion, NSTE-ACS escalation, pharmacotherapy and discharge safety-netting.
learningObjectives: Select the correct reperfusion or invasive timing pathway.
Apply antithrombotic safety checks and discharge prevention measures.
pitfalls: Missing posterior, high-lateral or right-ventricular occlusion patterns.
Mixing troponin assays for serial deltas.
Giving Prasugrel before coronary anatomy in NSTE-ACS.
Starting antithrombotics before excluding aortic dissection.
keyPoints: Obtain ECG within 10 minutes and search for ACOMI patterns.
Do not delay reperfusion for routine laboratory or troponin results.
Exclude aortic dissection before antithrombotic escalation.

patientEducation: Call emergency medical services immediately if chest pain recurs.
Adhere to DAPT and secondary-prevention medicines.
Stop smoking and address diet, diabetes, physical activity and rehabilitation.
lifestyleAndDiet: Smoking cessation, dietary optimisation, diabetes control, physical activity and cardiac rehabilitation.
mdtReferrals: Cardiology and catheter-lab activation, Coronary Care Unit (CCU), cardiac rehabilitation and relevant critical-care teams.
dischargeCriteria: Low-risk pathway with non-ischaemic serial ECGs and negative serial hs-cTn, or completed inpatient management and revascularisation.
Stable haemodynamics for at least 24–48 hours, secondary prevention optimised and DAPT education completed.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Arrange cardiology or CCU follow-up within 2–4 weeks and enrol in an accredited cardiac rehabilitation programme; arrange non-invasive testing when indicated by the risk pathway.
